stories.headline: Schumer accused of yearlong plot to plant 'decoy' candidate in critical Senate race
stories.note: The Alaska spoiler scandal now reaches toward Senate Democrats' top leader.
body: Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso of Wyoming, the chamber's No. 2 Republican, says he believes Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer helped drive the alleged scheme to put a second "Dan Sullivan" on Alaska's Senate ballot.

According to New York Times reporting, operatives for Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign and top aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee were involved in finding and recruiting a man with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. National Democrats say they had nothing to do with it.

Barrasso told Fox News Digital the plan amounted to criminal behavior and said Schumer "schemed and colluded" with the Peltola campaign for more than a year. Schumer's office and the Peltola campaign didn't respond to Fox's requests for comment.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski also condemned the tactic, writing that ballot-stacking has no place in elections. Because Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, both Sullivans, Peltola and Gerald Heikes will all appear on the same ballot. Peltola said Thursday in Juneau that she knew nothing about other candidates and isn't interested in tricking voters.
Why it matters: Tying the scandal to Schumer turns a local Alaska fight into a national story about Democratic leadership, just days before an Election Day where every Senate seat counts.

stories.headline: Dems' dire warnings about threats to democracy face an uncomfortable reckoning after Alaska election report
stories.note: The Alaska report undercuts Democrats' "threat to democracy" message days before the midterms.
body: Fox News Digital asked dozens of Democratic senators, House members and governors who endorsed Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola about the reported effort to confuse voters with a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot. As of publication, none had responded.

The list included lawmakers who have spoken loudly about protecting democracy, such as Sens. Richard Blumenthal, Chris Murphy and Cory Booker, along with Schumer, Adam Schiff, Elissa Slotkin, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Govs. Gavin Newsom and Wes Moore. Sen. John Fetterman has also stayed quiet.

The New York Times reported that Peltola aides helped recruit the other Sullivan, relying on text messages and interviews with former staffers. Peltola's campaign says it had no involvement with either Sullivan campaign. Separately, the Justice Department sued Alaska on Oct. 22 seeking to delay certification if the confusion could have changed the result, a case legal experts say faces real hurdles.
At least one Democrat has spoken up: Iowa gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand said both parties do this and "neither party should be doing it."
Why it matters: The silence undercuts Democrats' years-long "threat to democracy" message right before voters head to the polls.

stories.headline: 'Biscuit' the dog is latest dead felon to get their voting rights back from Spanberger, confused owner says
stories.note: A dog getting its voting rights restored makes Spanberger's rollout look even sloppier.
body: A Virginia constituent received an official certificate from Gov. Abigail Spanberger restoring the voting and jury-service rights of his dog, Biscuit, a beagle-hound mix from Goochland County that died about five years ago.

Republican Del. Tom Garrett, who got the letter from the owner, is calling for an independent audit of Spanberger's rights-restoration actions. He wants to know what databases and safeguards were used and how many certificates went to dead, nonexistent or duplicate people. It follows the earlier "Betty No Last Name" case in Chesapeake.
The owner, who asked not to be named, confirmed the letter to Fox News Digital and said Biscuit was never convicted of a felony "nor did she ever show any interest in voting."

A Spanberger spokesperson said the office "of course" didn't restore a dog's rights and that the record is tied to a person with a birthdate and Social Security number, but didn't answer follow-up questions. Spanberger has said about 100,000 people have had rights restored since she took office in January.
Why it matters: Virginians vote Tuesday on a Democrat-backed measure to make restoration automatic, and this episode raises fresh doubts about how carefully the current process is being run.

stories.headline: EXCLUSIVE: ICE captures illegal alien at center of NYC manhunt after sanctuary city release
stories.note: ICE closes the NYC manhunt and puts sanctuary policies back in the spotlight.
body: ICE officers arrested Alpha Bah, an illegal immigrant from Guinea accused of attacking a New York City police officer, on Friday afternoon, ending a manhunt that began after the city released him despite federal detainer requests.

A DHS official told Fox News Digital that officers tracked Bah to a temporary residence, held off approaching while school-age children were nearby, and then took him into custody without incident around 3:25 p.m. He was taken to 26 Federal Plaza in Manhattan for processing.

Bah was first arrested Oct. 7 on charges including aggravated assault on a police officer with a deadly weapon and resisting arrest. ICE had lodged a detainer at Queens Central Booking, but he was released without federal authorities being notified.
Before the arrest, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin blamed the city's sanctuary politicians and urged Gov. Kathy Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani to drop their "evil sanctuary policies."
Why it matters: The case gives Republicans a concrete example of sanctuary policies putting a suspect accused of violence back on the street, and of ICE cleaning it up.

stories.headline: Troubling discovery on state voter rolls sparks action days before midterms: 'Should have been fixed'
stories.note: A watchdog flagged thousands of possibly dead and duplicate voters in Maine right before the tight Collins Senate race, putting Democrat Shenna Bellows on the spot.
body: The conservative Public Interest Legal Foundation filed an election complaint in Maine on Tuesday, saying it found 3,181 potentially dead voters and 693 duplicate registrations on the state's rolls.

The complaint, filed with Democratic Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, argues the state hasn't made a reasonable effort to remove ineligible voters and asks for immediate corrective action under the federal Help America Vote Act. The group says it may appeal through that process if nothing is done.

Adams, speaking for the group, said the state, not an outside group, should be catching these problems. "It's something that should have been fixed a long time ago," he told Fox News Digital. The group's 2025 review found more than 18,000 potentially dead voters; Maine fixed many of those, but PILF says some errors remain and new ones have appeared.
PILF won a federal appeals case in 2024 forcing Maine to make its voter rolls public, and Adams accused Bellows of trying to keep the state's record out of public view.

Why it matters: Maine is days away from a tight Senate race between Republican Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson that could decide control of the Senate, and clean rolls are a core GOP election-integrity issue.

stories.headline: Liberal court delivers immigration win for Trump as judge warns of 'floodgates' if law firm succeeded
stories.note: Even the liberal Ninth Circuit sided with Trump, keeping the Diversity Visa lottery on hold.
body: In a 2-1 decision, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals blocked a lower-court order that would have forced the State Department to open applications for the 2027 Diversity Visa lottery, which admits about 55,000 immigrants a year.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio had delayed the application period last November, and the department later paused diversity visas indefinitely after a 2017 lottery-visa recipient carried out a deadly shooting at Brown University.

The appeals court found that the immigration law firm that sued, Red Eagle, had no standing, saying the program exists to encourage immigration, "not generate revenue for law firms." Letting the firm sue, the judges warned, would open "the floodgates."

The court stressed the ruling was procedural and that it did not endorse the department's failure to open registration. Former federal prosecutor Abhishek Kambli called the decision a "very easy call."
Why it matters: A win from the court that has blocked Trump on immigration many times keeps a program he has long opposed on hold heading into the midterms.

stories.headline: House Democrat declined request to seek Ilhan Omar ethics probe, newly obtained letter shows
stories.note: A newly obtained letter shows Rep. Angie Craig passed on a 2019 request to seek an Omar ethics probe, adding to Democrats' Omar headaches.
body: Correspondence obtained by Fox News Digital shows that in 2019, Rep. Angie Craig, a Minnesota Democrat, told then-state Rep. Steve Drazkowski he could file his own complaint with the Office of Congressional Ethics rather than seeking an investigation of Rep. Ilhan Omar herself.

Drazkowski, one of Craig's constituents, had asked her to forward his material to the House Ethics Committee. His concerns included that Omar filed joint tax returns with Ahmed Hirsi in 2014 and 2015 while she was still legally married to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.

His earlier complaints to the Minnesota Campaign Finance Board led to findings in June 2019 that Omar improperly used $1,500 in campaign money for personal tax services and had to repay some travel costs. Omar said at the time she was glad the process was over.

Drazkowski says he then filed his own ethics complaint and later took his information to the FBI's Minneapolis office, but never got a substantive response. Omar, Craig, the House Ethics Committee and the FBI didn't comment.
Why it matters: With Omar's past now under intense scrutiny, the letter raises questions about how Minnesota Democrats handled warnings years ago.
